result:
There is a peculiar hour in the morning when a city seems to belong to no one.

The traffic lights continue their patient rituals, changing for empty streets. Bakeries glow behind fogged windows. Somewhere, a delivery truck exhales at the curb while a lone cyclist passes through the blue-gray light. The buildings, usually crowded with purpose, stand quietly enough to reveal what they really are: enormous shelters filled with sleeping animals who have invented calendars, passwords, debts, lullabies, and names for the stars.

Soon, alarms will ring. Kettles will boil. People will remember their appointments and recover their worries. Doors will open, elevators will rise, and the streets will fill with millions of private worlds moving past one another.

But for a few minutes, everything waits.

I like the idea that stillness is not the absence of life but life between sentences—a breath held before the story continues.
